```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Instructor setup, hidden from the page.
# Let PROJ download datum-shift grids from cdn.proj.org. Without them, an
# NAD27 -> NAD83 conversion can silently fall back to a zero shift (see the
# "Behind the scenes" box in section 3). freeze: auto in _quarto.yml saves the
# results, so this only needs the network when the page is re-rendered.
sf::sf_proj_network(TRUE)

# Wider printed output, so data frames don't wrap on the page
options(width = 90)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// ---- Shared data and helpers for every widget on this page ----

// World countries and land (Natural Earth via the world-atlas package)
tc = require("topojson-client@3.1.0")
worldTopo = FileAttachment("countries-110m.json").json()
land = tc.feature(worldTopo, worldTopo.objects.land)
countries = tc.feature(worldTopo, worldTopo.objects.countries).features

// Colors used across widgets
col = ({
  ocean: "#eef3f7", land: "#cfc9bc", grid: "#c3ced8", ink: "#33414d",
  red: "#d1495b", blue: "#1f5f8b", orange: "#e08a1e", green: "#5b8c5a"
})

// Boxes to fit maps to. Mercator can't show the poles (they're infinitely
// far away), so its world view stops at 60° S and 84° N.
naBox = d3.geoGraticule().extent([[-128, 18], [-62, 56]]).outline()
mercBox = d3.geoGraticule().extent([[-180, -60], [180, 84]]).outline()
fitTarget = view => view === "na" ? naBox : view === "merc" ? mercBox : {type: "Sphere"}
```

## Today

- Tell a **geographic** CRS from a **projected** one in R's printout
- Explain what a **datum** is, and when datum differences matter
- Explain why every flat map **distorts** something, and choose a projection
  that protects what you measure
- Use **EPSG codes** to name, check, and convert CRSs

---

## 1 The failure, again

- Same failure as your homework, on new data: Luxembourg
- Elevation raster + 12 cantons (districts), both included with `terra`
- Scenario: the national mapping agency sends the elevation in its own grid,
  **EPSG:2169**

```{r}
#| label: libraries
#| warning: false
#| message: false
library(sf)       # vector data
library(terra)    # raster data
library(dplyr)    # filter() and friends
library(spData)   # the `world` dataset, used in section 4
library(units)    # converting m^2 to km^2, used in section 4
```

```{r}
#| label: load
# Elevation raster for Luxembourg
elev_file <- system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra")
elev <- rast(elev_file)

# The 12 cantons of Luxembourg, as sf polygons
cantons_file <- system.file("ex/lux.shp", package = "terra")
cantons <- st_read(cantons_file)
```

```{r}
#| label: make-national-grid
# Set up the scenario: the elevation in Luxembourg's national grid.
# (project() converts a raster between CRSs; more on it in a later session.)
elev_lux <- project(elev, "EPSG:2169")
elev_lux
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Predict

Compare the raster's `extent` with the cantons' `Bounding box`. If we draw the
cantons on top of the elevation, what will we see?
:::

```{r}
#| label: overlay-fail
#| fig-height: 5
# Raster first, cantons on top in red
plot(elev_lux)
plot(st_geometry(cantons), add = TRUE, border = "red")
```

```{r}
#| label: crop-fail
#| error: true
# Loud failure: crop() checks that the layers overlap, and stops
crop(elev_lux, cantons)
```

```{r}
#| label: extract-fail
# Silent failure: a mean elevation for each canton... all NaN
# (na.rm = TRUE is needed because elev.tif has no-data cells along the border)
bad <- extract(elev_lux, cantons, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
bad
```

**Three symptoms:**

- The plot shows **nothing**: no error, no warning
- `crop()` **stops** with an error
- `extract()` returns **all NaN**: no error, no warning

## 2 Geographic vs. projected CRSs

### Geographic CRS: positions are angles

```{=html}
<div class="widget" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(240px,1fr));gap:1rem;text-align:center">
  <!-- Latitude: a cross-section through the poles -->
  <svg viewBox="0 0 260 250" style="width:100%;max-width:300px;margin:auto">
    <circle cx="130" cy="125" r="90" fill="#eef3f7" stroke="#33414d" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <line x1="30" y1="125" x2="230" y2="125" stroke="#7a8ca3" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
    <line x1="130" y1="25" x2="130" y2="225" stroke="#7a8ca3" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
    <line x1="130" y1="125" x2="187.85" y2="56.06" stroke="#d1495b" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <circle cx="187.85" cy="56.06" r="5" fill="#d1495b"/>
    <path d="M165,125 A35,35 0 0,0 152.5,98.2" fill="none" stroke="#d1495b" stroke-width="2"/>
    <text x="170" y="112" font-size="14" fill="#d1495b">φ</text>
    <text x="130" y="18" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#33414d">N</text>
    <text x="130" y="242" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#33414d">S</text>
    <text x="232" y="120" font-size="11" text-anchor="end" fill="#33414d">equator</text>
    <circle cx="130" cy="125" r="3" fill="#33414d"/>
  </svg>
  <!-- Longitude: looking down on the North Pole -->
  <svg viewBox="0 0 260 250" style="width:100%;max-width:300px;margin:auto">
    <circle cx="130" cy="125" r="90" fill="#eef3f7" stroke="#33414d" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <line x1="130" y1="125" x2="130" y2="215" stroke="#7a8ca3" stroke-width="2"/>
    <line x1="130" y1="125" x2="207.9" y2="170" stroke="#1f5f8b" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <circle cx="207.9" cy="170" r="5" fill="#1f5f8b"/>
    <path d="M130,160 A35,35 0 0,0 160.3,142.5" fill="none" stroke="#1f5f8b" stroke-width="2"/>
    <text x="150" y="172" font-size="14" fill="#1f5f8b">λ</text>
    <circle cx="130" cy="125" r="3" fill="#33414d"/>
    <text x="130" y="115" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#33414d">N pole</text>
    <text x="130" y="232" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#33414d">Greenwich (0°)</text>
  </svg>
  <div style="grid-column:1/-1;display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(240px,1fr));gap:1rem;font-size:.95rem">
    <div><b style="color:#d1495b">Latitude φ</b>: angle north or south of the equator, measured at Earth's center (side view)</div>
    <div><b style="color:#1f5f8b">Longitude λ</b>: angle east or west of Greenwich (view from above the North Pole)</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

- Units: **degrees** (angles, not distances)
- Longitude −180° to 180°; latitude −90° to 90°
- Examples: **WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)**, NAD83 (EPSG:4269)

### Projected CRS: positions are distances on a flat grid

```{=html}
<div class="widget" style="text-align:center">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 560 250" style="width:100%;max-width:640px">
    <!-- Small globe with a patch highlighted -->
    <circle cx="90" cy="125" r="70" fill="#eef3f7" stroke="#33414d" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <ellipse cx="90" cy="125" rx="70" ry="18" fill="none" stroke="#c3ced8"/>
    <ellipse cx="90" cy="125" rx="30" ry="70" fill="none" stroke="#c3ced8"/>
    <path d="M100,80 L130,78 L134,105 L104,108 Z" fill="#d1495b" fill-opacity=".35" stroke="#d1495b"/>
    <!-- Arrow: flatten -->
    <path d="M170,125 L230,125" stroke="#33414d" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrowhead)"/>
    <text x="200" y="115" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#33414d">flatten</text>
    <defs>
      <marker id="arrowhead" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto">
        <path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 Z" fill="#33414d"/>
      </marker>
    </defs>
    <!-- Flat grid in meters -->
    <g transform="translate(260,30)">
      <rect x="0" y="0" width="260" height="180" fill="#fff" stroke="#33414d"/>
      <g stroke="#e3e8ee">
        <line x1="52" y1="0" x2="52" y2="180"/><line x1="104" y1="0" x2="104" y2="180"/>
        <line x1="156" y1="0" x2="156" y2="180"/><line x1="208" y1="0" x2="208" y2="180"/>
        <line x1="0" y1="36" x2="260" y2="36"/><line x1="0" y1="72" x2="260" y2="72"/>
        <line x1="0" y1="108" x2="260" y2="108"/><line x1="0" y1="144" x2="260" y2="144"/>
      </g>
      <line x1="0" y1="180" x2="270" y2="180" stroke="#33414d" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <line x1="0" y1="180" x2="0" y2="-8" stroke="#33414d" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <circle cx="0" cy="180" r="4" fill="#33414d"/>
      <text x="4" y="198" font-size="11" fill="#33414d">origin (0, 0)</text>
      <circle cx="160" cy="70" r="5" fill="#d1495b"/>
      <line x1="160" y1="70" x2="160" y2="180" stroke="#d1495b" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
      <line x1="160" y1="70" x2="0" y2="70" stroke="#d1495b" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
      <text x="160" y="214" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#d1495b">x = 77,000 m (easting)</text>
      <text x="6" y="62" font-size="12" fill="#d1495b">y = 75,000 m (northing)</text>
    </g>
  </svg>
</div>
```

- Flattens one part of the globe onto a plane (a **projection**)
- Units: **meters** (sometimes feet), measured from the grid's **origin**
- Built on top of a geographic CRS
- Examples: **EPSG:2169** (Luxembourg), **EPSG:5070** (NLCD), UTM zones

### A degree is not a fixed distance

- 1° of latitude ≈ **111 km** everywhere
- 1° of longitude **shrinks toward the poles**, because the meridians converge

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Predict

How long is 1° of longitude at Luxembourg (49.6° N)? More or less than 100 km?
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof lat = Inputs.range([0, 89], {
  value: 0.4, step: 0.1, label: "Latitude (° N)"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Length of one degree on a sphere of radius 6,371 km.
// Latitude: constant. Longitude: shrinks with cos(latitude).
kmPerDegLat = 111.2
kmPerDegLon = 111.2 * Math.cos(lat * Math.PI / 180)

// Reference places in Africa and Europe, so they all fit on one globe
places = [
  {name: "Libreville (equator)", lon: 9.45, lat: 0.4},
  {name: "Cairo", lon: 31.24, lat: 30.0},
  {name: "Luxembourg", lon: 6.13, lat: 49.6},
  {name: "Oslo", lon: 10.75, lat: 59.9},
  {name: "Svalbard", lon: 15.63, lat: 78.2}
]

{
  const wide = width > 720;
  const g = wide ? 300 : Math.min(width, 340);

  // ---- Wireframe globe: graticule, the chosen parallel, and the places ----
  const projection = d3.geoOrthographic().rotate([-15, -35]).fitExtent([[6, 6], [g - 6, g - 6]], {type: "Sphere"});
  const path = d3.geoPath(projection);
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", [0, 0, g, g]).style("width", g + "px");
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path({type: "Sphere"})).attr("fill", col.ocean).attr("stroke", col.ink);
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(land)).attr("fill", col.land).attr("fill-opacity", 0.6);
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(d3.geoGraticule().step([15, 15])()))
    .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.grid).attr("stroke-width", 0.7);
  // The full parallel at the slider's latitude: a smaller circle near the pole
  const parallel = {type: "LineString", coordinates: d3.range(-180, 181, 2).map(x => [x, lat])};
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(parallel)).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.red).attr("stroke-width", 2.5);
  // A 10-degree stretch of longitude (red) and of latitude (gray), to compare
  const seg = (a, b) => ({type: "LineString", coordinates: d3.range(0, 1.001, 0.05).map(t => [a[0] + t * (b[0] - a[0]), a[1] + t * (b[1] - a[1])])});
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(seg([10, Math.min(lat, 79)], [20, Math.min(lat, 79)])))
    .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.red).attr("stroke-width", 7).attr("stroke-linecap", "round");
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(seg([-10, Math.min(lat, 79)], [-10, Math.min(lat, 79) + 10])))
    .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#7a8ca3").attr("stroke-width", 7).attr("stroke-linecap", "round");
  for (const p of places) {
    const [x, y] = projection([p.lon, p.lat]);
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x).attr("cy", y).attr("r", 4).attr("fill", col.ink);
  }

  // ---- Bars: 1 degree of latitude vs. 1 degree of longitude ----
  const bw = wide ? Math.max(200, width - g - 60) : width - 20;
  const bar = (label, km, color) => html`
    <div style="margin:.35rem 0">
      <div style="font-size:.95rem">${label}: <b>${km.toFixed(1)} km</b></div>
      <div style="height:18px;width:${(km / kmPerDegLat) * bw}px;background:${color};border-radius:3px"></div>
    </div>`;

  // Buttons that move the slider. Built with DOM calls because Quarto's
  // html`` template doesn't attach functions as event handlers.
  const buttons = places.map(p => {
    const b = document.createElement("button");
    b.textContent = p.name;
    b.className = "btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary";
    b.style.margin = ".2rem .3rem .2rem 0";
    b.addEventListener("click", () => {
      const input = viewof lat;
      input.value = p.lat;
      input.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
    });
    return b;
  });

  return html`<div class="widget" style="display:${wide ? "grid" : "block"};grid-template-columns:${g}px 1fr;gap:1.5rem;align-items:center">
    <div>${svg.node()}</div>
    <div>
      ${bar("1° of latitude (gray)", kmPerDegLat, "#7a8ca3")}
      ${bar("1° of longitude (red)", kmPerDegLon, col.red)}
      <div style="margin-top:.6rem;font-size:.9rem">Jump to: ${buttons}</div>
      <div style="margin-top:.6rem;font-size:.85rem;color:#5f6b75">Thick segments on the globe span 10°. The red line is the full parallel at this latitude.</div>
    </div>
  </div>`;
}
```

- Lengths, areas, and buffers **in degrees are meaningless**
- `sf` computes areas and distances on the globe for you (`st_area()` gives
  m² even for lon/lat data)
- Not every function does: a raster's cell size stays in degrees

### Reading it in R

```{r}
#| label: geographic-check
# Is it longitude/latitude (degrees)?
st_is_longlat(cantons)   # sf objects
is.lonlat(elev_lux)      # terra rasters

# The ranges of the coordinates tell the same story
st_bbox(cantons)
ext(elev_lux)
```

- Cantons span about **0.8 degrees** east–west
- The raster spans about **57,000 meters**
- Same country, different units, so the numbers **don't overlap** (section 1
  explained)

## 3 Datums and ellipsoids

- **Ellipsoid**: a smooth mathematical shape (size + flattening)
- **Datum**: an ellipsoid + **where it's pinned** to the real Earth
- Change the datum and the **same lat/lon** points to a **different spot**

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
datumSteps = [
  "1 · The real Earth",
  "2 · An ellipsoid",
  "3 · NAD27: pinned in Kansas",
  "4 · Satellites",
  "5 · WGS 84: Earth-centered"
]
viewof datumStep = Inputs.radio(datumSteps, {value: datumSteps[0], label: "Step"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// ---- Datum animation: geometry, built once. A separate cell (below)
// moves things around when the step changes, with transitions. ----
datumGeom = {
  const W = 640, H = 380;
  const earth = {x: 430, y: 195};             // Earth's center of mass
  // The lumpy "real" Earth (a geoid, hugely exaggerated): a wobbly radius
  const rEarth = th => 118 * (1 + 0.05 * Math.sin(3 * th + 0.5) + 0.035 * Math.cos(5 * th) + 0.02 * Math.sin(8 * th + 1));
  const earthPath = d3.line().curve(d3.curveCardinalClosed)(
    d3.range(0, 2 * Math.PI, Math.PI / 60).map(th => [earth.x + rEarth(th) * Math.cos(th), earth.y - 0.9 * rEarth(th) * Math.sin(th)])
  );
  // Meades Ranch, Kansas: a point on the upper left of the cross-section
  const thPin = 125 * Math.PI / 180;
  const pin = [earth.x + rEarth(thPin) * Math.cos(thPin), earth.y - 0.9 * rEarth(thPin) * Math.sin(thPin)];
  // Clarke 1866 (NAD27): placed so its surface passes through the pin
  const nad27 = {rx: 100, ry: 82};
  nad27.x = pin[0] - nad27.rx * Math.cos(thPin);
  nad27.y = pin[1] + nad27.ry * Math.sin(thPin);
  // WGS 84: centered on Earth's center of mass, a best fit everywhere
  const wgs84 = {rx: 121, ry: 104, x: earth.x, y: earth.y};
  const start = {rx: 112, ry: 94, x: 140, y: 195};  // ellipsoid parked on the left
  return {W, H, earth, earthPath, pin, nad27, wgs84, start};
}

datumSvg = {
  const {W, H, earth, earthPath, pin, start} = datumGeom;
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", [0, 0, W, H]).style("width", "100%").style("max-width", "720px");

  // Movement uses CSS transitions (set by the step cell below), which run in
  // every browser without a JavaScript animation loop
  const fade = "opacity 1s ease";
  const glide = "transform 1.4s ease, opacity 1s ease";

  // Satellite orbit (dashed) and a satellite circling Earth's center
  const sat = svg.append("g").attr("id", "sat").style("opacity", 0).style("transition", fade);
  sat.append("circle").attr("cx", earth.x).attr("cy", earth.y).attr("r", 170)
    .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#9aa5ad").attr("stroke-dasharray", "3 5");
  const craft = sat.append("g");
  craft.append("rect").attr("x", earth.x - 6).attr("y", earth.y - 176).attr("width", 12).attr("height", 12).attr("fill", col.ink);
  craft.append("rect").attr("x", earth.x - 26).attr("y", earth.y - 173).attr("width", 18).attr("height", 6).attr("fill", col.blue);
  craft.append("rect").attr("x", earth.x + 8).attr("y", earth.y - 173).attr("width", 18).attr("height", 6).attr("fill", col.blue);
  craft.append("animateTransform").attr("attributeName", "transform").attr("type", "rotate")
    .attr("from", `0 ${earth.x} ${earth.y}`).attr("to", `-360 ${earth.x} ${earth.y}`)
    .attr("dur", "9s").attr("repeatCount", "indefinite");

  // The lumpy Earth and its center of mass
  svg.append("path").attr("d", earthPath).attr("fill", "#cfe0d2").attr("stroke", col.green).attr("stroke-width", 2);
  svg.append("g").attr("id", "earthCenter").call(g => {
    g.append("path").attr("d", `M${earth.x - 7},${earth.y}h14M${earth.x},${earth.y - 7}v14`).attr("stroke", col.green).attr("stroke-width", 2.5);
    g.append("text").attr("x", earth.x + 10).attr("y", earth.y + 18).attr("font-size", 12).attr("fill", col.green).text("center of mass");
  });

  // Ghost of the NAD27 ellipsoid, shown in the last step for comparison
  const {nad27} = datumGeom;
  svg.append("ellipse").attr("id", "ghost").attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.red)
    .attr("stroke-dasharray", "5 4")
    .attr("cx", nad27.x).attr("cy", nad27.y).attr("rx", nad27.rx).attr("ry", nad27.ry)
    .style("opacity", 0).style("transition", fade);

  // The ellipsoid, with its semi-major (a) and semi-minor (b) axes.
  // The outer group moves it; the inner group scales it to each datum's size
  // (non-scaling-stroke keeps the outline the same thickness).
  const ell = svg.append("g").attr("id", "ell")
    .style("opacity", 0).style("transform", `translate(${start.x}px, ${start.y}px)`).style("transition", glide);
  ell.append("g").attr("id", "shape").style("transition", glide)
    .append("ellipse").attr("rx", start.rx).attr("ry", start.ry)
    .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.red).attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("vector-effect", "non-scaling-stroke");
  ell.append("circle").attr("r", 3.5).attr("fill", col.red);
  const axes = ell.append("g").attr("id", "axes").style("transition", fade);
  axes.append("line").attr("x2", start.rx).attr("stroke", col.red).attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
  axes.append("line").attr("y2", -start.ry).attr("stroke", col.red).attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
  axes.append("text").attr("x", start.rx / 2).attr("y", 16).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 14).attr("fill", col.red).text("a");
  axes.append("text").attr("x", 8).attr("y", -start.ry / 2).attr("font-size", 14).attr("fill", col.red).text("b");
  axes.append("text").attr("x", 0).attr("y", start.ry + 26).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 12).attr("fill", col.ink)
    .text("a = equatorial radius, b = polar radius");

  // Meades Ranch pin
  const pinG = svg.append("g").attr("id", "pin").style("opacity", 0).style("transition", fade);
  pinG.append("path").attr("d", `M${pin[0]},${pin[1]} l-7,-16 a8,8 0 1,1 14,0 z`).attr("fill", col.red).attr("stroke", "#fff");
  pinG.append("text").attr("x", pin[0] - 14).attr("y", pin[1] - 24).attr("text-anchor", "end").attr("font-size", 12).attr("fill", col.ink)
    .text("Meades Ranch, Kansas");

  // The figure plus a caption line (filled in by the step cell below)
  return html`<div class="widget" style="text-align:center">${svg.node()}
    <div class="datum-caption" style="font-size:1.05rem;font-weight:500;margin-top:.3rem"></div></div>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// ---- Move things for the chosen step (re-runs when the step changes) ----
{
  const s = datumSteps.indexOf(datumStep) + 1;
  const {nad27, wgs84, start} = datumGeom;
  const svg = d3.select(datumSvg);

  // Where the ellipsoid sits and how big it is at each step. Setting these
  // styles triggers the CSS transitions defined when the figure was built.
  const e = s <= 2 ? start : s <= 4 ? nad27 : wgs84;
  svg.select("#ell").style("opacity", s >= 2 ? 1 : 0)
    .style("transform", `translate(${e.x}px, ${e.y}px)`);
  svg.select("#shape").style("transform", `scale(${e.rx / start.rx}, ${e.ry / start.ry})`);
  svg.select("#axes").style("opacity", s === 2 ? 1 : 0);
  svg.select("#pin").style("opacity", s >= 3 ? 1 : 0);
  svg.select("#sat").style("opacity", s >= 4 ? 1 : 0);
  svg.select("#ghost").style("opacity", s === 5 ? 0.8 : 0);

  const captions = [
    "The real Earth is lumpy (shape hugely exaggerated)",
    "An ellipsoid: a smooth shape we can do math on",
    "NAD27 (Clarke 1866): fits North America, pinned at one survey point. Its center is NOT Earth's center",
    "Satellites orbit Earth's center of mass, so we can now locate that center",
    "WGS 84: centered on Earth's center of mass. Dashed = NAD27. Same lat/lon, different place"
  ];
  svg.select(".datum-caption").text(captions[s - 1]);
  // Nothing to display from this cell (the figure lives in the cell above)
  return html`<span></span>`;
}
```

| Datum | Ellipsoid | Pinned to | Where you'll meet it |
|---|---|---|---|
| NAD27 | Clarke 1866 | Survey point in Kansas (Meades Ranch) | Old maps and surveys |
| NAD83 | GRS 80 | Earth's center (moves with North America) | Census / TIGER, state agencies |
| WGS 84 | WGS 84 | Earth's center (global) | GPS, web data, EPA TRI |

### How much does it matter?

Same coordinates for the AU campus, labeled NAD27 vs. NAD83:

```{r}
#| label: datum-shift
# One pair of numbers: longitude, latitude
au_xy <- st_point(c(-77.0887, 38.9365))

# The same numbers, labeled with two different datums
au_nad27 <- st_sfc(au_xy, crs = 4267)
au_nad83 <- st_sfc(au_xy, crs = 4269)

# Convert the NAD27 point to NAD83, so both are on one datum
au_nad27_converted <- st_transform(au_nad27, 4269)

# How far apart are "the same" coordinates on the ground?
st_distance(au_nad83, au_nad27_converted)
```

- NAD27 vs. NAD83: **≈ 28 m**, enough to cross a street or a tract boundary
- NAD83 vs. WGS 84: **≈ 1–2 m** in the US, rarely matters for tracts or 30 m
  rasters
- R treats **any** CRS difference as a mismatch, so TRI points (WGS 84) must
  still be transformed to join Census tracts (NAD83)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Behind the scenes: datum shifts need extra files

- Accurate NAD27 → NAD83 conversion uses a grid of measured shifts, downloaded
  separately
- If PROJ (the library under `sf` and `terra`) can't find it, it falls back to
  a "ballpark" conversion, which can mean **zero shift, no error**
- This page was built with `sf_proj_network(TRUE)`, which lets PROJ fetch grids
  as needed
- The general lesson: running without an error isn't proof it did what you
  think
:::

---

## 4 Projections: flattening is a trade

### Families: what you project onto

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  // Three schematic diagrams (sphere + surface, with projection rays),
  // each above the real graticule that family produces.
  const pw = 220, ph = 340;
  const cx = 110, cy = 110, r = 55;

  function base(svg) {
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", r).attr("fill", col.ocean).attr("stroke", col.ink).attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
    svg.append("ellipse").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("rx", r).attr("ry", 10).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.grid);
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", 2.5).attr("fill", col.ink);
  }
  // A ray from the sphere's center, through the sphere, to the surface
  function ray(svg, x2, y2) {
    const a = Math.atan2(y2 - cy, x2 - cx);
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", cx).attr("y1", cy).attr("x2", x2).attr("y2", y2).attr("stroke", col.orange).attr("stroke-width", 1.3);
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", cx + r * Math.cos(a)).attr("cy", cy + r * Math.sin(a)).attr("r", 3).attr("fill", col.orange);
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x2).attr("cy", y2).attr("r", 3.5).attr("fill", col.red);
  }
  // The graticule this family produces, drawn in the lower part of the panel
  function grat(svg, projection) {
    const box = [[20, 215], [pw - 20, ph - 30]];
    projection.fitExtent(box, {type: "Sphere"});
    const path = d3.geoPath(projection);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path({type: "Sphere"})).attr("fill", col.ocean).attr("stroke", col.ink);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(land)).attr("fill", col.land);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(d3.geoGraticule().step([30, 30])())).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.grid);
  }
  function panel(title, note, draw, projection) {
    const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", [0, 0, pw, ph]).style("width", "100%").style("max-width", "260px");
    draw(svg);
    grat(svg, projection);
    svg.append("text").attr("x", pw / 2).attr("y", ph - 8).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 12).attr("fill", col.ink).text(note);
    return html`<div style="text-align:center"><div style="font-weight:600">${title}</div>${svg.node()}</div>`;
  }

  const cylinder = panel("Cylindrical", "touches along the equator", svg => {
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", cx - r).attr("y1", 20).attr("x2", cx - r).attr("y2", 200).attr("stroke", col.blue).attr("stroke-width", 2);
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", cx + r).attr("y1", 20).attr("x2", cx + r).attr("y2", 200).attr("stroke", col.blue).attr("stroke-width", 2);
    svg.append("ellipse").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", 20).attr("rx", r).attr("ry", 9).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.blue).attr("stroke-width", 2);
    svg.append("ellipse").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", 200).attr("rx", r).attr("ry", 9).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.blue).attr("stroke-width", 2);
    base(svg);
    svg.append("ellipse").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("rx", r).attr("ry", 10).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.red).attr("stroke-width", 2);
    ray(svg, cx + r, cy - r * Math.tan(30 * Math.PI / 180));
    ray(svg, cx + r, cy - r * Math.tan(50 * Math.PI / 180));
    ray(svg, cx - r, cy + r * Math.tan(35 * Math.PI / 180));
  }, d3.geoEquirectangular());

  const cone = panel("Conic", "touches along one parallel", svg => {
    // Cone tangent to the sphere at 35° N; apex on the axis above the pole
    const phi = 35 * Math.PI / 180;
    const tx = cx + r * Math.cos(phi), ty = cy - r * Math.sin(phi);
    const apexY = ty - (tx - cx) / Math.tan(phi);
    const baseY = 165, baseX = tx + (baseY - ty) * Math.tan(phi);
    base(svg);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", `M${2 * cx - baseX},${baseY} L${cx},${apexY} L${baseX},${baseY}`).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.blue).attr("stroke-width", 2);
    svg.append("ellipse").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", baseY).attr("rx", baseX - cx).attr("ry", 11).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.blue).attr("stroke-width", 2);
    svg.append("ellipse").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", ty).attr("rx", tx - cx).attr("ry", 7).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.red).attr("stroke-width", 2);
    // Rays hit the cone's side: intersect each ray with the cone line
    for (const deg of [15, 55]) {
      const a = -deg * Math.PI / 180;
      const dx = Math.cos(a), dy = Math.sin(a);
      // Cone side: from apex (cx, apexY) toward (baseX, baseY)
      const ux = baseX - cx, uy = baseY - apexY;
      const den = dx * uy - dy * ux;
      const s = ((cx - cx) * uy - (apexY - cy) * ux) / den;
      ray(svg, cx + s * dx, cy + s * dy);
    }
  }, d3.geoConicEqualArea().parallels([30, 50]));

  const plane = panel("Azimuthal (planar)", "touches at one point", svg => {
    base(svg);
    const py = cy - r;
    svg.append("path").attr("d", `M${cx - 85},${py + 10} L${cx - 45},${py - 10} L${cx + 85},${py - 10} L${cx + 45},${py + 10} Z`)
      .attr("fill", col.blue).attr("fill-opacity", 0.08).attr("stroke", col.blue).attr("stroke-width", 2);
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", py).attr("r", 4).attr("fill", col.red);
    for (const deg of [60, 115]) {
      const a = deg * Math.PI / 180;
      ray(svg, cx + (cy - py) / Math.tan(a), py);
    }
  }, d3.geoAzimuthalEquidistant().rotate([0, -90]));

  return html`<div class="widget" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(200px,1fr));gap:1rem">${cylinder}${cone}${plane}</div>`;
}
```

- **Red** = where the surface touches the globe: **least distortion** there
- Distortion **grows** with distance from the red line or point
- Conic suits mid-latitude areas wider than tall: the **US, Maryland**

### Properties: what a projection preserves

**First choice: pick one (no map can do both)**

- **Equal-area**: areas correct, shapes stretched
- **Conformal**: local shapes and angles correct, areas stretched
- Or a **compromise**: neither exactly, both errors kept moderate (good for
  world maps to look at)

**Extras: true only from one point or along certain lines**

- **Equidistant**: distances from the center point are correct
- **Azimuthal**: directions from the center point are correct (all planar
  projections have this, hence the family name)
- Extras combine with the first choice: e.g. Lambert *azimuthal equal-area*

**Choose by what your analysis measures**

### Explore: distortion across projections

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Predict

The red circles are all the same size on the globe. On Mercator, how will the
polar circles compare with those at the equator? On Equal Earth?
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Tissot circles: identical 4-degree circles on a 30 x 15 degree grid
tissot = {
  const circles = [];
  for (let lon = -180; lon < 180; lon += 30) {
    for (let lat = -75; lat <= 75; lat += 15) {
      circles.push(d3.geoCircle().center([lon, lat]).radius(4)());
    }
  }
  return {type: "GeometryCollection", geometries: circles};
}

// Two routes from DC to London. Great circle = shortest path on the globe.
// Rhumb line = constant compass bearing: a straight line on Mercator, so we
// build it by drawing a straight line in Mercator space and un-projecting it.
dc = [-77.04, 38.90]
london = [-0.13, 51.51]
greatCircle = ({type: "LineString", coordinates: [dc, london]})
rhumbLine = {
  const m = d3.geoMercator();
  const [x0, y0] = m(dc), [x1, y1] = m(london);
  const coords = d3.range(0, 1.0001, 0.01).map(t => m.invert([x0 + t * (x1 - x0), y0 + t * (y1 - y0)]));
  return {type: "LineString", coordinates: coords};
}

// ---- The projections on offer, with the facts shown in the info card ----
projections = new Map([
  ["Equirectangular (plain lon/lat)", {
    make: () => d3.geoEquirectangular(), view: "world", family: "Cylindrical",
    keeps: "Neither (distance along meridians only)",
    gives: "Area and shape, badly near the poles",
    epsg: "What you get when you plot EPSG:4326 data as x/y",
    use: "Quick looks. Not for measuring."
  }],
  ["Mercator", {
    make: () => d3.geoMercator(), view: "merc", family: "Cylindrical",
    keeps: "Conformal: shapes and angles",
    gives: "Area: grows rapidly toward the poles",
    epsg: "3857 (Web Mercator, used by web maps), 3395",
    use: "Navigation, web basemaps. Never for area."
  }],
  ["Equal Earth", {
    make: () => d3.geoEqualEarth(), view: "world", family: "Pseudocylindrical",
    keeps: "Equal-area",
    gives: "Shape, especially near the edges",
    epsg: "8857",
    use: "World maps of anything per area."
  }],
  ["Albers Equal Area Conic (US)", {
    make: () => d3.geoConicEqualArea().parallels([29.5, 45.5]).rotate([96, 0]),
    view: "na", family: "Conic", keeps: "Equal-area",
    gives: "Shape, slightly, away from the two standard parallels",
    epsg: "5070 (NAD83 / Conus Albers, used by NLCD)",
    use: "Areas and densities across the US."
  }],
  ["Lambert Conformal Conic (Maryland)", {
    make: () => d3.geoConicConformal().parallels([38.3, 39.45]).rotate([77, 0]),
    view: "na", family: "Conic", keeps: "Conformal",
    gives: "Area, growing away from Maryland's latitudes",
    epsg: "26985 (NAD83 / Maryland, m), 2248 (same, US feet)",
    use: "State Plane: Maryland agency data."
  }],
  ["Transverse Mercator (UTM zone 18N)", {
    make: () => d3.geoTransverseMercator().rotate([75, 0]),
    view: "na", family: "Cylindrical (turned sideways)", keeps: "Conformal",
    gives: "Scale grows east and west of 75° W",
    epsg: "26918 (NAD83 / UTM 18N), 32618 (WGS 84 / UTM 18N)",
    use: "Distances and buffers in DC, MD, VA."
  }],
  ["Azimuthal Equidistant (centered on DC)", {
    make: () => d3.geoAzimuthalEquidistant().rotate([77.04, -38.9]),
    view: "world", family: "Azimuthal",
    keeps: "Distance and direction from DC",
    gives: "Area and shape, worst far from DC",
    epsg: "No standard code; defined around any center",
    use: "\"How far is everything from here?\""
  }],
  ["Orthographic (a view of the globe)", {
    make: () => d3.geoOrthographic().rotate([77.04, -38.9]), view: "world",
    family: "Azimuthal (perspective)", keeps: "Looks like the globe from space",
    gives: "Shows only half the Earth",
    epsg: "Rarely used for analysis",
    use: "Reference: compare the others with this one."
  }]
])
```

```{ojs}
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(land)).attr("fill", col.land);
  if (layers.includes("Tissot circles")) {
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(tissot)).attr("fill", col.red).attr("fill-opacity", 0.55);
  }

    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(greatCircle)).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.blue).attr("stroke-width", 2.5);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(rhumbLine)).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.orange).attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("stroke-dasharray", "6 4");
  }
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path({type: "Sphere"})).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#9aa5ad");

  const legend = layers.includes("Routes: DC → London")
    ? html`<div style="font-size:.9rem;margin-top:.3rem"><span style="color:${col.blue}">━━</span> great circle (shortest) &nbsp; <span style="color:${col.orange}">╍╍</span> rhumb line (constant compass bearing)</div>`
    : "";

  // Each fact is its own <div> so the card can flow into columns
  const card = html`<dl class="proj-card">
    <div><dt>Family</dt><dd>${p.family}</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Preserves</dt><dd>${p.keeps}</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Gives up</dt><dd>${p.gives}</dd></div>
    <div><dt>EPSG codes</dt><dd>${p.epsg}</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Use it for</dt><dd>${p.use}</dd></div>
  </dl>`;
  return html`<div class="widget">${svg.node()}${legend}${card}</div>`;
}
```

- **Mercator vs. Equal Earth**: which keeps the circles' *size*? Their *shape*?
- **Two conic maps over Maryland**: nearly identical. Locally, a *sensible*
  CRS matters more than the *perfect* one

### Why sailors used Mercator

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Route facts: distances and bearings for both routes (sphere, R = 6,371 km)
routeFacts = {
  const R = 6371, rad = Math.PI / 180;
  const [l1, p1] = dc.map(v => v * rad), [l2, p2] = london.map(v => v * rad);
  // Compass bearing from a to b at the start of a great circle
  const bearing = (la1, ph1, la2, ph2) => {
    const y = Math.sin(la2 - la1) * Math.cos(ph2);
    const x = Math.cos(ph1) * Math.sin(ph2) - Math.sin(ph1) * Math.cos(ph2) * Math.cos(la2 - la1);
    return (Math.atan2(y, x) / rad + 360) % 360;
  };
  const gcStart = bearing(l1, p1, l2, p2);
  const gcEnd = (bearing(l2, p2, l1, p1) + 180) % 360;
  const gcKm = d3.geoDistance(dc, london) * R;
  // Rhumb line: one bearing the whole way
  const dPsi = Math.log(Math.tan(Math.PI / 4 + p2 / 2) / Math.tan(Math.PI / 4 + p1 / 2));
  const rhumbBearing = (Math.atan2(l2 - l1, dPsi) / rad + 360) % 360;
  const rhumbKm = Math.abs((p2 - p1) / Math.cos(rhumbBearing * rad)) * R;
  return {gcStart, gcEnd, gcKm, rhumbBearing, rhumbKm};
}

{
  const wide = width > 700;
  const w = wide ? Math.floor((width - 40) / 2) : width;
  const h = Math.round(w * 0.8);
  function panel(title, projection, fit) {
    projection.fitExtent([[6, 6], [w - 6, h - 6]], fit).clipExtent([[0, 0], [w, h]]);
    const path = d3.geoPath(projection);
    const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", [0, 0, w, h]).style("width", "100%");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path({type: "Sphere"})).attr("fill", col.ocean).attr("stroke", "#9aa5ad");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(d3.geoGraticule10())).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.grid).attr("stroke-width", 0.5);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(land)).attr("fill", col.land);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(greatCircle)).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.blue).attr("stroke-width", 3);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(rhumbLine)).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.orange).attr("stroke-width", 3).attr("stroke-dasharray", "7 4");
    for (const pt of [dc, london]) {
      const [x, y] = projection(pt);
      svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x).attr("cy", y).attr("r", 4.5).attr("fill", col.ink);
    }
    return html`<div><div style="font-weight:600">${title}</div>${svg.node()}</div>`;
  }
  // North Atlantic box for Mercator; the globe view centers on the Atlantic
  const atlantic = d3.geoGraticule().extent([[-95, 20], [15, 65]]).outline();
  const f = routeFacts;
  return html`<div class="widget">
    <div style="display:${wide ? "grid" : "block"};grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:1rem">
      ${panel("Mercator", d3.geoMercator(), atlantic)}
      ${panel("Globe (orthographic)", d3.geoOrthographic().rotate([40, -45]), {type: "Sphere"})}
    </div>
    <table class="table table-sm" style="margin-top:.75rem;font-size:.95rem">
      <thead><tr><th></th><th>Distance</th><th>Compass bearing</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td style="color:${col.blue}"><b>Great circle</b> (solid)</td><td>${Math.round(f.gcKm).toLocaleString()} km</td>
          <td>starts ${Math.round(f.gcStart)}°, ends ${Math.round(f.gcEnd)}°: <b>always changing</b></td></tr>
        <tr><td style="color:${col.orange}"><b>Rhumb line</b> (dashed)</td><td>${Math.round(f.rhumbKm).toLocaleString()} km</td>
          <td><b>${Math.round(f.rhumbBearing)}° the whole way</b></td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>`;
}
```

- Mercator is **conformal**: the Tissot circles stay **round**, so angles are
  true everywhere (only sizes change)
- So a **constant compass bearing** (rhumb line) is a **straight line** on
  Mercator
- Navigator: draw a straight line, measure its angle, steer that bearing
- The catch: the rhumb line is **longer**; the shortest route needs a
  constantly changing bearing

### How big is Greenland, really?

- Drag Greenland south; the DRC (blue) stays put
- Greenland's **true size never changes**

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof targetLat = Inputs.range([0, 73], {
  value: 73, step: 1, label: "Greenland's center latitude (° N)"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Move a country along its own meridian to a new center latitude by rotating
// it on the globe. Rotation keeps its true size and shape.
function moveTo(feature, newLat) {
  const [lon0, lat0] = d3.geoCentroid(feature);
  const toOrigin = d3.geoRotation([-lon0, -lat0]);   // centroid -> (0, 0)
  const toTarget = d3.geoRotation([-lon0, -newLat]); // (lon0, newLat) -> (0, 0)
  const move = pt => toTarget.invert(toOrigin(pt));
  const walk = c => typeof c[0] === "number" ? move(c) : c.map(walk);
  return {type: "Feature", geometry: {
    type: feature.geometry.type, coordinates: walk(feature.geometry.coordinates)
  }};
}

greenland = countries.find(d => d.properties.name === "Greenland")
drc = countries.find(d => d.properties.name === "Dem. Rep. Congo")
movedGreenland = moveTo(greenland, targetLat)

{
  const wide = width > 700;
  const w = wide ? Math.floor((width - 40) / 2) : width;
  const h = Math.round(w * 0.75);

  // Draw one panel and report Greenland's apparent size relative to the DRC
  function panel(title, makeProjection, view) {
    const projection = makeProjection().fitExtent([[6, 6], [w - 6, h - 6]], fitTarget(view));
    const path = d3.geoPath(projection);
    const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", [0, 0, w, h]).style("width", "100%");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path({type: "Sphere"})).attr("fill", col.ocean);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(land)).attr("fill", "#dcd8cf");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(greenland))
      .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col.red).attr("stroke-dasharray", "3 3");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(drc)).attr("fill", col.blue);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(movedGreenland)).attr("fill", col.red);
    const looks = path.area(movedGreenland) / path.area(drc);
    return html`<div>
      <div style="font-weight:600">${title}</div>${svg.node()}
      <div>Greenland looks <span class="readout">${looks.toFixed(1)}×</span> the DRC</div>
    </div>`;
  }

  // True ratio, measured on the globe
  const truth = d3.geoArea(greenland) / d3.geoArea(drc);

  return html`<div class="widget">
    <div style="display:${wide ? "grid" : "block"};grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:1rem">
      ${panel("Mercator (conformal)", d3.geoMercator, "merc")}
      ${panel("Equal Earth (equal-area)", d3.geoEqualEarth, "world")}
    </div>
    <p style="margin:.75rem 0 0">On the globe: Greenland = <b>${truth.toFixed(2)}×</b> the DRC, anywhere.
      Dashed outline = Greenland's real location.</p>
  </div>`;
}
```

The same comparison in R:

```{r}
#| label: areas
# `world` (from spData) is in EPSG:4326
two <- filter(world, name_long %in% c("Greenland", "Democratic Republic of the Congo"))

# The same two countries in two projected CRSs
two_merc <- st_transform(two, 3857)   # Web Mercator
two_ee   <- st_transform(two, 8857)   # Equal Earth

# Area on the globe (sf does this for lon/lat data), then on each flat map
area_globe <- st_area(two)
area_merc  <- st_area(two_merc)
area_ee    <- st_area(two_ee)

# Convert from square meters to square kilometers
area_globe <- set_units(area_globe, km^2)
area_merc  <- set_units(area_merc, km^2)
area_ee    <- set_units(area_ee, km^2)

data.frame(country = two$name_long, area_globe, area_merc, area_ee)
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Discuss

- Every number above was computed correctly. Which would you report?
- What would an AI report if it "helpfully" transformed to 3857 first?
:::

---

## 5 EPSG codes: names for CRSs

- One number = a complete CRS: datum + ellipsoid + projection + units
- Registry maintained by IOGP: [epsg.org](https://epsg.org) (official),
  [epsg.io](https://epsg.io) (easier to search)
- Look a code up: `https://epsg.io/` + the number

| EPSG | Name | Type | Units | Where you'll see it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [4326](https://epsg.io/4326) | WGS 84 | Geographic | degrees | GPS, web data, EPA TRI |
| [4269](https://epsg.io/4269) | NAD83 | Geographic | degrees | Census tracts via `tidycensus` |
| [4267](https://epsg.io/4267) | NAD27 | Geographic | degrees | Old maps and surveys |
| [3857](https://epsg.io/3857) | WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator | Projected, cylindrical | "meters" (stretched) | Web map tiles. Display only |
| [5070](https://epsg.io/5070) | NAD83 / Conus Albers | Projected, conic, equal-area | meters | NLCD; areas across the US |
| [26918](https://epsg.io/26918) | NAD83 / UTM zone 18N | Projected, transverse Mercator | meters | Distances in DC, MD, VA |
| [32618](https://epsg.io/32618) | WGS 84 / UTM zone 18N | Projected, transverse Mercator | meters | Same zone, WGS 84 datum (GPS data) |
| [26985](https://epsg.io/26985) | NAD83 / Maryland | Projected, Lambert conic | meters | Maryland state data |
| [2248](https://epsg.io/2248) | NAD83 / Maryland (ftUS) | Projected, Lambert conic | **US feet** | Maryland county GIS. Check units! |

### Reading a CRS in R

```{r}
#| label: read-epsg
# Short summary: name, code, and where it's meant to be used
crs("EPSG:26985", describe = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: read-wkt
# The full definition (called WKT). Skim for these four things:
#   the name on the first line (PROJCRS = projected; GEOGCRS = geographic)
#   DATUM and ELLIPSOID
#   METHOD (the projection)
#   LENGTHUNIT under AXIS (the units of x and y)
st_crs(26985)
```

- First line: **PROJCRS** (projected) or **GEOGCRS** (geographic)
- **DATUM / ELLIPSOID**: which model of the Earth
- **METHOD**: which projection
- **LENGTHUNIT**: meters or feet?

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Choose a CRS

Pick a code from the table and defend it in one sentence:

1. Total impervious area in each Maryland county
2. TRI facilities within 1 km of each Baltimore tract centroid
3. Asthma prevalence across the 48 contiguous states
4. An interactive web map for a community group
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Some defensible answers

1. **5070** (equal-area) or **26985**: within one state, State Plane's area
   distortion is tiny. The *why* is the point
2. **26985**, **26918**, or **32618**: meters, accurate locally. Not 4326:
   a 1 km buffer needs meters
3. **5070**: equal-area across the country
4. **3857** for *display*. Analyze in a measuring CRS, then transform for the
   map
:::

---

## 6 Back to the failure: fix it and check it

**Why it failed**

- Cantons: coordinates around **6 and 50** (degrees)
- Raster: coordinates in the **tens of thousands** (meters)
- `plot()` just draws numbers: cantons landed far outside the raster's
  extent
- `crop()`: no overlap → **stops**
- `extract()`: no cells inside any polygon → `NaN`, **silently**

**The fix**

- Put both layers in **one CRS**
- Transform the **vector** to match the raster: moving vertices is exact,
  while reprojecting a raster resamples cell values

```{r}
#| label: fix
# Convert the cantons into the raster's CRS
cantons_lux <- st_transform(cantons, crs(elev_lux))

# Check 1: do the two CRSs now match?
st_crs(cantons_lux) == st_crs(elev_lux)

# Check 2: are the coordinate ranges now comparable?
st_bbox(cantons_lux)
ext(elev_lux)
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-plot
#| fig-height: 5
# Check 3: look at it
plot(elev_lux)
plot(st_geometry(cantons_lux), add = TRUE, border = "red")
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-extract
# The zonal mean now works: one number per canton
good <- extract(elev_lux, cantons_lux, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
cantons_lux$elev_mean <- good$elevation

# Check 4: no missing values, and plausible elevations (meters)
sum(is.na(cantons_lux$elev_mean))
summary(cantons_lux$elev_mean)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Labeling is not converting

- `st_transform()` **converts**: the numbers change
- `st_set_crs()` / `st_crs(x) <- ...` only **relabels**: the numbers stay
- Relabel only when a file has **no** CRS and you **know** what it should be
- AI assistants sometimes suggest relabeling as a "fix" for a mismatch:

```{r}
#| label: relabel-trap
# Wrong: claims the degrees are now meters
cantons_relabeled <- st_set_crs(cantons, 2169)
st_bbox(cantons_relabeled)
```

- R warns, and the bbox gives it away: still 5.7 to 50.2
- In EPSG:2169, numbers that small sit at the grid's origin: in France, about
  120 km southwest of Luxembourg's center
:::

---

## 7 In your code

| Question | Function | What to look for |
|---|---|---|
| What CRS is this? | Print the object; `st_crs(x)`; `crs(r, describe = TRUE)` | Name, EPSG code, units |
| Degrees or meters? | `st_is_longlat(x)`; `is.lonlat(r)` | `TRUE` means degrees |
| Do my layers match? | `st_crs(a) == st_crs(b)`; compare `st_bbox()` and `ext()` | Same CRS; ranges that overlap |
| Does it look right? | `plot()` the raster, then the vector with `add = TRUE` | Lines where you expect them |
| Convert a vector | `st_transform(x, crs)` | The bbox numbers change |
| Convert a raster | `project(r, crs)` | Resamples values (later session) |
| Label a CRS-less file | `st_set_crs(x, crs)` | Only when the CRS is missing *and* known |

- **Check the CRS before** combining two layers; **check the result after**
- Most CRS mistakes don't produce errors. They produce **wrong answers**

## 8 Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. A bounding box reads `xmin: 316268 ymin: 4295630 xmax: 334407 ymax: 4318264`. Degrees or meters? Projected or geographic?

- Meters, so projected: longitudes stop at ±180, latitudes at ±90
- Hundreds of thousands and millions look like UTM (this is Washington, DC,
  in UTM zone 18N)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. `extract(r, polygons, fun = mean)` gives you some `NaN`s. Name three possible causes, and how you'd tell them apart.

- **All NaN**: the layers don't overlap. Usually a **CRS mismatch** (today's
  failure); sometimes the raster covers a different area. Compare `st_bbox()`
  and `ext()`
- **Some NaN, with `na.rm = TRUE`**: those polygons fall only on **no-data
  cells** or **outside the raster's edge**. Plot the polygons on the raster
  and look at where the NaN ones are
- **Many NaN, without `na.rm = TRUE`**: any polygon that touches even **one
  no-data cell** returns NaN. Here, 9 of 12 cantons did. Add `na.rm = TRUE`,
  and decide whether a partial average is acceptable
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. An AI suggests `st_transform(tri, 2263)` before buffering TRI facilities in Baltimore by 1,000. Look up [EPSG:2263](https://epsg.io/2263). What's wrong?

- It's **NAD83 / New York Long Island (ftUS)**: the wrong place, and the units
  are **US feet**
- A buffer of 1,000 would be 1,000 ft (about 305 m), not 1 km
- Baltimore is outside its area of use, so distortion is larger too
- Better: **26985** (Maryland, meters) or **26918 / 32618** (UTM 18N)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. TRI facilities are in EPSG:4326 and tracts in EPSG:4269, about a meter apart. What happens if you `st_join()` them without transforming? Loud or silent?

- **Loud**: `st_join()` stops with `st_crs(x) == st_crs(y) is not TRUE`
- `sf` requires identical CRSs and can't judge whether a meter matters for your
  question
- Fix: transform one to match the other (or both to a projected CRS you'll
  measure in)
- Compare with `extract()` in section 1, which failed **silently**
:::
